title: The “Three Options” technique
description: This text describes a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) technique for working with negative automatic thoughts called “Three Options.” It helps broaden your perspective on a situation and reduce anxiety by intentionally considering the worst, best, and most realistic outcomes. Regular practice can help reduce the intensity of negative emotions.

texts: <activitylink id="kdzYJ4njVJ">
CBT offers many simple and useful tools for working with negative automatic thoughts.

Some techniques help you notice these thoughts, while others help you check them for logic and reduce how much you believe them. Most exercises can be done on your own to help maintain your mental well-being. In this chapter, we’ll share a tool that is excellent for breaking the cycle of rumination. It’s called the “Three Options” technique.

If you’ve already learned to catch thoughts that hit hard, you’ve likely noticed that many of them are irrational and don’t align with the facts—yet we still tend to believe them and don’t always know how to handle them.

The main goal of this technique is to broaden your perspective and show your mind that there are other possibilities beyond the anxious scenario. Through this process, you’ll learn to question negative thoughts and reduce anxiety in stressful situations.
So, what do you do? The scheme is simple. As soon as you notice a thought that has ruined your mood, ask yourself: how could things play out?
• The worst — the most unpleasant option, which is usually the first one that comes to mind;
• The best — the ideal outcome that would satisfy you completely;
• The most realistic — the middle ground between the first two: a balanced scenario based on experience and facts;

A key detail: it’s better to write these scenarios down rather than just keeping them in your head. You can do this on your phone or on paper — whichever is more convenient. Writing them down helps you look at the situation more objectively.
Enough theory — let’s look at an example.
Suppose you have an important exam at school or work tomorrow, and the thought pops up: “I’m going to fail.”
There’s no guarantee of the outcome, but the thought is already causing anxiety. So, let’s give your brain some alternatives.

The absolute worst: I won’t prepare well, I’ll panic during the exam, and I’ll fail. Even worse — I’ll be the only one in the group who didn’t make it. The instructor will be disappointed, and my classmates will think I’m lazy and disorganized.
The absolute best: I’ll arrive at the exam calmly, get an easy topic, and ace it. Even better — if the whole group gets top marks without even having to take the exam.

The most realistic: I don’t know which topic I’ll get, but I can review the difficult subjects today — that will make me feel calmer tomorrow. A little nervousness is normal. Overall, I know the material and can answer most questions. The instructor is friendly toward me, and there’s no reason to fail. I’ll refresh my knowledge on the tricky parts in the morning and feel more confident. Most likely, I’ll pass with at least a satisfactory grade, and if I stay focused, I’ll get a good or excellent grade.
<q author="Viktor Frankl">Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our freedom to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.</q>

test.question: What is the main goal of the “Three Options” technique in CBT?
answers: To help make quick decisions in difficult situations
To eliminate all negative thoughts and replace them with positive ones
To broaden your perspective on a situation and see alternative outcomes
To speed up the problem-solving process without thinking about consequences

texts: This approach provides at least three outcomes — though in reality, there may be more.
It is helpful to think of a “backup plan” in advance in case the worst-case scenario happens.
This significantly lowers the emotional intensity: even if the worst happens, you will know how to act.
For example: if I do fail the exam tomorrow, I can take a retake. It would be unpleasant, but I’ll dedicate another day or two to studying — and fix the situation.

<important>It is unlikely that my instructor or classmates will fundamentally change their attitude toward me because of one failure; and if they do, it only shows what their attitude is actually worth.</important>
With this approach, the situation no longer feels terrifying, and the thought no longer feels like the only option.
It might seem like this is either too simple or, conversely, too long and tedious to write everything out.
But practice shows that this technique truly works as a self-help tool — which is exactly why we are recommending it to you.
